title: Real word parts, checked against a reference
statement: Check every word-part split, affix meaning and pronunciation against a dictionary or rule-based reference, never intuition, because invented splits teach false word-parts.
example: Checked against a rule-based reference, 5 of 23 authored word-part splits were flagged, two of them teaching a flatly wrong rule.
detail: Verifying a course's 23 authored word-part splits against a rule-based reference flagged 5 for review: two taught a flatly wrong rule on screen, two were folk splits and one was defensible but non-standard (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0213-qc-week-0902-0904.qmd`, lines 49-66). The course's QC checklist, which counts all 5 as wrong, now requires every split checked that way, never by intuition, with words that don't decompose taught as word families (`grade3-reading/artifacts/AlphaRead-QC-Checklist-v2-2026-09-04.md`, row L2). Reviews found affix glosses that over-generalise, such as '-ing means it is happening right now' for two descriptive words, and a gloss built on a verb that doesn't exist, 'one who stranges' (`grade3-reading/artifacts/peter-pan-standing-2026-09-11/PP-STANDING.md`; `grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-inceptbench-2026-09-29/REGISTER.md`), and an audit found a suffix printed without its hyphen, which a young reader takes for the insect (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-inceptbench-2026-09-30/REGISTER.md`). A calibration log ranks this class, content correctness against an outside authority, as the most frequent judgment machines couldn't make: 4 hits across all 9 logged rounds (`grade3-reading/artifacts/cert-layer/AUTOMATED-CHECKS-ROADMAP-2026-08-31.md`). Teach only real word parts: print each affix with its hyphen, and teach a word that doesn't split as a word family.
against: No verified morpheme reference was in the repository to diff against, so the class was judged not automatable honestly (`grade3-reading/artifacts/cert-layer/AUTOMATED-CHECKS-ROADMAP-2026-08-31.md`). the word-part tool generates its splits by rule rather than looking them up, so its own verdicts need the same check. One lesson's rule, recorded in walkthroughs that have since been superseded.

prefix/suffix reference list covers ~90% of multisyllabic words the course will teach; the remaining ~10% (and judgment calls even within the covered 90%) require HUMAN judgment — morpheme analysis has no formulaic AI approach, because Latin, Greek, and Old English root patterns vary in ways a fixed rule set will not reliably catch.
Do not attempt to fully automate morpheme-split generation; treat the prefix/suffix list as the high-coverage starting reference, not a replacement for a human pass.
